questions.q: Communication is described as:
o: A two-way process involving a sender and a receiver
A one-way process from manager to employee
A process that needs no receiver
questions.d: Communication: a two-way, dynamic process with a sender and a receiver; every communication carries a message.
questions.w: The slides' MCQ also gives 'two-way process' as the answer.

questions.q: Robbins says organisational communication involves exchanging and understanding information to promote:
questions.d: Organisational communication (Robbins, 2014): the exchange and understanding of information within an organization.
questions.w: Its purpose is coordination, better decisions and relationships.

questions.q: In the communication process, which step comes right after idea generation?
questions.d: Steps: idea generation → encoding → choosing the channel → transmission → receiving → decoding → feedback, while addressing noise.
questions.w: After forming the idea, the sender must put it into words or symbols.

questions.q: Converting the sender's thoughts into words, pictures, gestures or symbols is:
questions.d: Encoding: converting messages into communication symbols the receiver can understand.
questions.w: Decoding is the receiver translating those symbols back into meaning.

questions.q: The receiver interpreting and understanding the encoded message is:
questions.d: Decoding: translating the encoded message into a language the receiver understands.
questions.w: The slides' MCQ calls it the 're-translation of signals into ideas'.

questions.q: The path or channel through which a message is sent, such as email, telephone or face-to-face, is the:
questions.d: Media: the path, channel or medium that carries the encoded message.
questions.w: Media is the carrier of the message.

questions.q: The receiver's reaction sent back to the sender, showing the message was received and understood, is:
questions.d: Feedback: the reversal of communication; the receiver expresses a reaction to the sender.
questions.w: Feedback completes the communication loop.

questions.q: A poor internet connection, an inattentive receiver and faulty decoding are examples of:
questions.d: Noise: any obstruction or hindrance in the communication process, affecting sender, message, media or receiver.
questions.w: Anything that distorts the message is noise.

questions.q: Gestures, facial expressions, glances and smiles are:
questions.d: Non-verbal communication: communication without words, often called body language.
questions.w: No words are used, so it is non-verbal.

questions.q: Signs, typography, graphic design, illustrations and animation are:
questions.d: Visual communication: using visual elements to convey ideas and information.
questions.w: These are designed images, not body language.

questions.q: According to the slides, written communication is:
o: More formal but less efficient than oral communication, and useful for legal documents
questions.d: Written communication: typically more formal but less efficient than oral; useful for legal documents; e.g. emails and text messages.
questions.w: Its formality suits records and legal matters.

questions.q: A manager giving instructions to subordinates is:
questions.d: Downward communication: from superiors to subordinates. Upward: from subordinates to superiors.
questions.w: The message flows down the hierarchy.

questions.q: A field salesperson communicating directly with the Vice President of HR is:
questions.d: Diagonal communication: cuts across hierarchical barriers between different levels and departments.
questions.w: The slides use exactly this example for diagonal communication.

questions.q: Communication between people working at the same level in an organization is:
questions.d: Horizontal communication: between persons at the same level.
questions.w: Neither person is above the other.

questions.q: Communication between an organization and others outside it is:
questions.d: External communication: between the organization and outsiders. Internal: within the organization.
questions.w: The other party is outside the organization.

questions.q: Low self-confidence, lack of enthusiasm and a mismatch between verbal and non-verbal messages are:
questions.d: Sender-centric barriers: resistance to change, low confidence, lack of motivation, poor communication skills, verbal/non-verbal mismatch, insufficient training.
questions.w: These problems start with the person sending the message.

questions.q: Selective perception, prejudice and lack of interest in the topic are:
questions.d: Receiver-centric barriers: selective perception, unwillingness to change, lack of interest, prejudice and beliefs, personal values, here-and-now factors.
questions.w: These problems are in the person receiving the message.

questions.q: Venue noise, room temperature, poor timing and technological issues are:
questions.d: External barriers: environment, limited time or poor timing, technological issues, attitudes of customers, suppliers and competitors.
questions.w: These come from the surroundings, not the people or the organization's structure.

questions.q: Silos created by functional specialization, rigid policies and a lack of suggestion boxes or meetings are:
questions.d: Organisational barriers: functional specialization, rigid policies and rules, lack of communication facilities.
questions.w: They come from how the organization is structured and run.

questions.q: A manager who stresses punctuality and always arrives on time, setting a clear standard, uses which method?
questions.d: Communication through actions: actions speak louder than words; consistency builds trust.
questions.w: The manager's behaviour reinforces the message.

questions.q: Avoiding technical terms, words with more than one meaning and difficult symbols is:
questions.d: Using proper language: simple, meaningful language to avoid semantic distortion.
questions.w: Clear words prevent misunderstanding.

questions.q: Managers using the grapevine without ignoring official channels is:
questions.d: Judicious use of the grapevine: informal channels can help, but official channels must not be ignored.
questions.w: The grapevine should support, not replace, formal communication.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the 7Cs of effective communication?
questions.d: 7Cs: be clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous.
questions.w: Creativity is useful, but it is not one of the 7Cs.

questions.q: Which is a way to communicate effectively, according to the slides?
o: Adapting your communication style to the listeners
questions.d: How to communicate effectively: active listening, giving and receiving constructive feedback, adapting style to listeners, volume and clarity, understanding non-verbal messages.
questions.w: The other options are habits that block effective communication.

questions.q: Communication is a one-way process.
questions.d: Communication is a two-way process involving a sender and a receiver.
questions.w: Feedback from the receiver makes it two-way.

questions.q: Upward communication flows from subordinates to superiors.
questions.d: Upward communication: subordinates to superiors. Downward: superiors to subordinates.
questions.w: The message moves up the hierarchy.

questions.q: Informal communication takes place within the formal organization, between its members.
questions.d: Informal communication: takes place within the formal organization between members; formal communication is official.
questions.w: It happens alongside official channels, e.g. the grapevine.

questions.q: Noise can affect only the receiver.
questions.d: Noise: a hindrance that may affect the sender, message, media or receiver.
questions.w: Noise can enter at any point in the process.

questions.q: Feedback is important because communication is a two-way process.
questions.d: Feedback ensures the receiver has received and understood the message.
questions.w: Without feedback the sender cannot know whether the message was understood.

questions.q: Effective communication helps mitigate and control conflicts within the organization.
questions.d: Importance of effective communication: bridges stakeholders, builds relationships, expresses thoughts and goals, improves interactions, controls conflict.
questions.w: Clear communication prevents misunderstandings that cause conflict.

questions.q: Describe the steps in the communication process.
questions.a:
1. Idea generation: the sender identifies the need to communicate and forms the idea.
2. Encoding: the sender translates the idea into a suitable form (words, symbols).
3. Choosing the channel: the sender selects the most effective medium.
4. Transmission: the sender delivers the message through the channel.
5. Receiving: the receiver gets the message.
6. Decoding: the receiver interprets and tries to understand it.
7. Feedback: the receiver responds, completing the loop.
8. Addressing noise: both parties reduce disruptions for clarity.
questions.d: Communication process: the sequence of steps by which a message moves from sender to receiver and back.
questions.w: The process is a loop: feedback returns to the sender.

questions.q: Explain the eight elements of the communication process.
questions.a:
1. Sender: initiates communication using effective verbal and non-verbal techniques.
2. Message: ideas, feelings, suggestions or orders, oral or written; should be clear.
3. Encoding: converting the message into symbols (words, pictures, gestures).
4. Media: the channel carrying the message (face to face, phone, letter, email, internet).
5. Decoding: translating the symbols into meaning the receiver understands.
6. Receiver: the recipient (a person, a machine or an audience).
7. Feedback: the receiver's reaction; confirms understanding.
8. Noise: any hindrance affecting sender, message, media or receiver (e.g. poor connection, inattentive receiver).
questions.d: Elements of communication: the parts that make up the communication process.
questions.w: Define each element briefly and give an example where possible.

questions.q: Explain the four categories of communication.
questions.a:
1. Verbal communication: using words and language, oral or written (speaking, listening, reading, writing).
2. Written communication: more formal but less efficient than oral; useful for legal documents; e.g. emails and text messages.
3. Non-verbal communication: without words; body language such as gestures, facial expressions, glances, smiles.
4. Visual communication: using visual elements such as signs, typography, graphic design, illustration, advertising and animation.
questions.d: Categories of communication: verbal, written, non-verbal and visual.
questions.w: Each category differs by the means used to carry the message.

questions.q: Explain the types of business communication.
questions.a:
- Internal: information flow within the organization.
- External: between the organization and outsiders.
- Formal: official communication.
- Informal: within the formal organization between members (e.g. grapevine).
- Downward: superiors to subordinates.
- Upward: subordinates to superiors.
- Horizontal: between people at the same level.
- Diagonal: across hierarchical levels and departments (e.g. a field salesperson to the VP of HR).
questions.d: Business communication: the flow of information within and outside an organization.
questions.w: Group the types in pairs (internal/external, formal/informal) and by direction of flow.

questions.q: Explain the four types of communication barriers with examples.
questions.a:
1. Sender-centric: resistance to change, low self-confidence, lack of enthusiasm, poor communication skills, verbal/non-verbal mismatch, insufficient feedback and training.
2. Receiver-centric: selective perception, unwillingness to change, lack of interest, prejudice and beliefs, personal values, here-and-now factors.
3. External: environment (venue, noise, temperature), limited or poor timing, technological issues, attitudes of customers, suppliers and competitors.
4. Organisational: functional specialization creating silos, rigid policies and rules, lack of communication facilities (meetings, suggestion boxes, open-door systems).
questions.d: Communication barriers: obstacles faced when trying to communicate effectively.
questions.w: Classify each barrier by where it comes from: sender, receiver, surroundings or organization.

questions.q: Explain how managers can overcome communication barriers, and list the 7Cs of effective communication.
questions.a:
Methods:
1. Employee orientation on objectives, policies, procedures and authority relations.
2. Improving interpersonal relations: respect subordinates to build trust.
3. Empathetic listening: let subordinates express feelings.
4. Using proper language: simple words; avoid technical terms.
5. Communication through actions: act consistently with your words.
6. Judicious use of the grapevine alongside official channels.
7. Giving and using feedback.
7Cs: be clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous.
questions.d: Personal effectiveness in communication: conveying messages clearly, listening actively and adapting styles for mutual understanding.
questions.w: Match each method to the barrier it removes, then add the 7Cs as personal guidelines.
